# Brain health and dementia

> *Patients with a family history of dementia often ask what to eat to avoid it, and the best-supported
> answer is control of vascular risk rather than a particular food or supplement. We cover the
> pathophysiology of neurodegeneration and small-vessel disease, how diet and vascular risk factors
> affect dementia risk, eating difficulties in advanced dementia, and when to refer.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how neurodegeneration and cerebral small-vessel disease add together to cause dementia, and
  why lowering the vascular load lowers the total burden.
- Explain why vascular risk control is the best-supported preventive approach, and interpret the Lancet
  Commission's "up to about 45%" estimate without overselling it.
- Distinguish the MIND diet's cohort association from its null prevention trial, and recommend a
  Mediterranean-style pattern as a low-risk choice.
- Evaluate brain supplements against the trial evidence, including those that can cause harm.
- Identify the non-dietary measures with good supporting evidence: physical activity, hearing and vision
  correction, and social and mental engagement.
- Recognise weight loss in advanced dementia as part of the illness, explain why tube feeding does not
  help, and refer for a goals-of-care conversation.
:::

## Brain health and dementia at a glance {#sec-overview}

**Dementia** is a clinical syndrome of acquired, progressive loss of memory and thinking severe enough
to affect daily life. Patients often hope for a dietary way to prevent it, and careful counselling
matters because the evidence is encouraging in one area and weak in the others. Four messages
summarise the evidence:

- The largest dietary benefit for the brain comes through vascular risk: what protects the heart
  protects the brain. Managing blood pressure, glucose, weight, lipids, smoking and activity is the
  best-supported, most actionable advice. It is the same prevention as for heart disease and diabetes
  (see the [*Cardiovascular disease & hypertension*](cardiovascular-disease-hypertension.qmd) and
  [*Type 2 diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapters).
- A brain-healthy eating pattern is a reasonable, low-risk choice, not a proven cure. The cohort
  studies look impressive, but the one prevention trial built to test a brain diet was negative.
- No brain supplement is proven to prevent dementia, and a few can do harm.
- Late in the disease the concern shifts from prevention to eating difficulty. Weight loss and
  difficulty eating are an expected part of advanced dementia, not a nutritional gap to fill with a
  feeding tube.

The task here is to recognise the modifiable risk factors, counsel truthfully and refer; no drug names
or doses are needed.

## Pathophysiology: neurodegeneration and small-vessel disease {#sec-dementia-pathways}

Two kinds of brain damage usually occur together in dementia.

The first is **neurodegeneration**: the accumulation of abnormal proteins, with loss of synapses and
neurons and brain atrophy. Two proteins accumulate: **amyloid-β**, in plaques between neurons, and
**tau**, in tangles inside them. Neurodegeneration is the dominant process in Alzheimer's disease.
Its exact causal chain is still debated, so the amyloid-and-tau account is the leading model, not
settled fact.

The second is vascular: damage to the brain's small blood vessels, called **cerebral small-vessel
disease**. Chronic hypertension damages blood vessels and drives stroke (see the
[*Cardiovascular disease & hypertension*](cardiovascular-disease-hypertension.qmd) chapter), and it
damages the brain's own small vessels too. Hypertension stiffens and thickens the small
arterioles, which impairs blood flow and injures the surrounding white matter. The result is the
**lacunar strokes** (small, deep infarcts: areas of brain tissue killed by a blocked small vessel)
and white-matter changes seen on scans.

Diabetes adds to the same vascular injury. The hyperglycaemic, insulin-resistant state (see the
[*Type 2 diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapter) also damages the brain's small vessels and speeds
brain atrophy [@biessels2014diabetesmri]. There is no separate "diabetic dementia".

![Two kinds of damage usually combine to produce dementia. Neurodegeneration (amyloid plaques and tau tangles) and cerebral small-vessel disease (from hypertension and diabetes) each push the brain toward a clinical threshold; because their injury adds together, reducing the vascular load lowers the total burden and can keep a person below that threshold for longer.](/figures/mechanisms/dementia-two-pathways.svg){#fig-two-pathways}

The two processes rarely occur alone. In older people with dementia, **mixed pathology**, more than one disease
process in the same brain, is the rule: in a community autopsy study, more than half of those who had
dementia had more than one pathology, most often Alzheimer changes plus infarcts
[@schneider2007mixed]. The safest reading is that the two kinds of damage add up: vascular injury
lowers the threshold at which neurodegeneration shows as dementia [@kapasi2017threshold].

::: {.example}
The Nun Study is the classic demonstration. Among nuns whose brains met the post-mortem criteria
for Alzheimer's disease, those who also had small strokes were more likely to have had dementia in
life, and fewer plaques and tangles seemed to be enough to produce it [@snowdon1997nunstudy].
:::

The additive model has a practical implication. We cannot yet clear plaques and tangles with food, but we
*can* reduce the vascular load, and doing so lowers the total burden whichever model of
neurodegeneration turns out to be right.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: food cannot yet clear amyloid plaques or tau tangles. Why can lowering vascular risk still delay dementia?
In older people, mixed pathology is the rule: neurodegeneration and cerebral small-vessel disease
often occur in the same brain. On the safest reading, the two kinds of damage add up, so vascular
injury lowers the threshold at which neurodegeneration shows as dementia, as in the Nun Study.
Reducing the vascular load lowers the total burden and can keep a person below that threshold for
longer, whichever model of neurodegeneration proves right.
:::

## Dietary management: reducing dementia risk {#sec-dementia-levers}

Vascular risk factors are the best-supported target for reducing dementia risk. The MIND diet's cohort association was not confirmed in a trial, no supplement is proven to prevent dementia, and some of the strongest preventive measures are not dietary.

### Vascular risk factors {#sec-dementia-vascular}

The cardiometabolic risk factors for heart disease (hypertension, diabetes, high LDL cholesterol,
obesity, smoking and physical inactivity) are also the modifiable risk factors for the vascular contribution
to dementia. Nutrition acts on the brain mostly *through* this vascular route, by improving those risk
factors.

The Lancet Commission estimates that up to about 45% of dementia is associated with a set of
modifiable factors across a lifetime [@livingston2024lancet]. The figure is a
**population-attributable estimate**: a theoretical ceiling that assumes these factors are fully causal
and could be eliminated from the whole population. The estimate is easy to oversell. It does not
mean that one person who controls their risk factors cuts their own risk by 45%, and it is not proof
from a trial.

Each risk factor raises risk only modestly, and reducing vascular damage is one of several ways the
factors are thought to act [@livingston2024lancet]. Because each effect is modest, the large number
comes from adding many common exposures across a life, not from one dominant cause. Two further
points help in interpreting the estimate. The largest single contributors in the model are hearing loss and high LDL cholesterol (about 7%
each), followed by less education and social isolation (about 5% each). Diet is not among the modelled
factors, because the Commission judged its evidence not consistent enough to include. Midlife is also a key period, so prevention is a long-term
effort.

The best trial evidence that treating a vascular risk factor protects the brain comes from SPRINT
MIND. Intensively lowering blood pressure significantly reduced **mild cognitive impairment** (a
decline in memory or thinking that falls short of dementia) and the combined measure of mild
impairment or dementia [@sprintmind2019jama]. It did not, on its own, reduce dementia (the trial was
stopped early for its heart benefit, leaving it underpowered for that harder endpoint). Even with that
caveat, it is the best trial evidence available, and it points to vascular risk.

### Can a diet prevent dementia? {#sec-dementia-diet}

The belief that a diet can prevent dementia comes from cohort studies. The **MIND diet** is a blend of
Mediterranean and DASH eating that emphasises leafy greens, berries, nuts, wholegrains, fish and olive
oil. In observational cohorts it was linked to a large reduction in Alzheimer's disease: roughly half
the risk in the highest-adherence group [@morris2015mindad]. The result is impressive, and widely
repeated as fact.

A three-year randomised trial of the MIND diet, built specifically to answer the prevention question,
then found no cognitive benefit over a control diet with the same mild calorie restriction and counselling
[@barnes2023mindrct]. The trial did not confirm the cohort association.

Three explanations could account for the difference (see the [*Evidence vs hype*](evidence-vs-hype.qmd) chapter):

- People who eat well differ in many other ways, some of which could produce the association.
  That is **confounding**: distortion of an association by a third factor linked to both the
  exposure and the outcome.
- Early, undiagnosed disease can dull appetite and worsen diet (reverse causation).
- Three years may be too short.

It is rarely possible to predict which promising observational findings a randomised trial will confirm.

<div data-island="trial-check" data-src="/diagrams/trial-check.yml"></div>

For a patient, a Mediterranean-style or MIND-style pattern is safe, affordable and good for the heart.
It is reasonable to recommend as a low-risk choice, though not as proven prevention of dementia.

**Multidomain programmes**, which combine diet, exercise, cognitive activity and vascular monitoring,
have improved cognitive test scores in trials such as FINGER [@ngandu2015finger]. Even the best of them
has not shown a reduction in dementia itself, and the benefit probably comes largely from the
vascular component.

### Do brain supplements prevent dementia? {#sec-dementia-supplements}

Patients often ask about supplements. No supplement is proven to prevent dementia, and
several carry a downside:

| Supplement | Claim / rationale | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| B vitamins | Lower homocysteine (an amino acid in the blood); a small study showed slower brain atrophy on scans [@smith2010vitacog] | Large trials found no benefit to memory or thinking [@clarke2014bvitamin]; an imaging change is not a clinical benefit |
| Fish-oil (omega-3) capsules | Omega-3 for the brain | Trials show no cognitive benefit [@sydenham2012cochraneomega3]; eat fish rather than taking capsules |
| Vitamin E | Antioxidant for prevention | Trials found it did not prevent dementia in older men [@kryscio2017preadvise] or stop mild impairment progressing to dementia [@farina2017vitaminecochrane]; at high doses it has been linked to a small increase in death [@miller2005vitamine], so this one can cause harm |
| Ginkgo biloba | The classic "brain tonic" | A large trial found it did not reduce dementia at all [@dekosky2008gem]; may raise bleeding risk in people taking blood thinners such as warfarin [@nccih2025ginkgo] |
| Coconut oil or "MCT" (medium-chain triglycerides) | Marketed for Alzheimer's | No credible trial evidence, and coconut oil is more than 80% saturated fat [@usdaFdcCoconutOil], so it works against the vascular risk control that actually matters |
| "Medical foods" | Marketed for memory | A regulatory category with a lower bar than a medicine; the label is not evidence that the product works |

A claim deserves scepticism when it rests on a blood or scan marker instead of memory itself, on a
small pilot, or on an after-the-fact subgroup.

### Non-dietary modifiable risk factors {#sec-dementia-beyond}

The worried-well patient should hear about all the options, and some of the strongest preventive measures are
not dietary:

- physical activity, a core recommendation for brain health that works partly through the same
  vessels (see the [*Healthy ageing*](healthy-ageing.qmd) chapter on exercise in older adults);
- correcting hearing and vision, which matters more than most people expect: uncorrected hearing loss
  is one of the largest single modifiable contributors to dementia risk, so "get your hearing and eyes
  checked" is concrete, useful advice.

Staying socially and mentally engaged, and treating depression and sleep problems, complete the
list. Building **cognitive reserve** (the brain's capacity to absorb damage before dementia shows)
and social reserve early also helps: greater reserve, together with less vascular damage, is thought
to be part of why age-specific dementia incidence has fallen in some high-income countries
[@livingston2024lancet].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does dementia-prevention advice lead with blood pressure and glucose, not with a brain diet?
Vascular risk control has the strongest trial evidence: in SPRINT MIND, intensive blood-pressure lowering
reduced mild cognitive impairment, although the trial was underpowered to show fewer cases of dementia
itself. Diabetes injures the same small vessels, so glucose control acts on the same vascular pathway.
The MIND diet's halved risk came from cohorts, which confounding and reverse causation can inflate,
and it was not confirmed in a three-year randomised trial. A Mediterranean-style pattern is still worth
recommending as a low-risk, heart-healthy choice, but not as proven prevention.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: B vitamins slowed brain atrophy on scans in a small study. Why is that not a reason to recommend them?
Brain atrophy on a scan is a marker, not memory itself. When B vitamins were tested in large trials,
they brought no benefit to memory or thinking. A claim that rests on a blood or scan marker, a small
pilot or an after-the-fact subgroup deserves scepticism.
:::

## Eating difficulties and weight loss in advanced dementia {#sec-dementia-advanced}

As dementia advances, weight loss and difficulty eating are expected, driven by the disease itself:
most people with advanced dementia develop an eating problem, and it marks a late stage of the illness
[@mitchell2009cascade]. The instinct, and the family's plea, is to "do something so she doesn't
starve", and a common ward response is to consider a feeding tube.

There are no randomised trials, and the observational evidence is of low certainty, but it shows no
sign of benefit. In advanced dementia, studies have found no evidence that tube feeding prolongs
survival, prevents aspiration pneumonia, heals or prevents pressure ulcers, or improves comfort, and it
is linked to harm, including *more* pressure ulcers [@davies2021cochranetubefeeding;
@teno2012pressureulcers]. Geriatrics societies and the Choosing Wisely campaign converge on the same
position: **careful hand feeding**, offering food for comfort, is preferred [@ags2014feedingtubes; @agscw2013fivethings].

The generalist's task is to recognise the trajectory and explain gently that the weight loss is part
of the illness and not neglect; the referral that follows is set out in
[When to refer](#sec-dementia-refer).

Two things are separate from the tube question and still appropriate: correcting a genuine vitamin
deficiency, and supporting oral intake with feeding help earlier in the disease.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why is the weight loss of advanced dementia not a gap that a feeding tube can close?
The weight loss and difficulty eating are driven by the disease itself and mark its late stage, so they
are not a simple shortfall of intake. In advanced dementia, tube feeding does not prolong survival,
prevent aspiration pneumonia, heal or prevent pressure ulcers, or improve comfort, and it is linked to
more pressure ulcers. Careful hand feeding for comfort, with a referral for a goals-of-care
conversation, is the evidence-based response.
:::

## When to refer {#sec-dementia-refer}

The generalist counsels on prevention and recognises the late-stage trajectory. Three situations call
for a referral instead of further advice or a product:

- Persistent worry about genetic risk. A patient with a family history may ask about genetic
  testing for the *APOE* gene, whose variants are linked to Alzheimer's risk. The answer is that *APOE*
  is not tested for or acted on in ordinary prevention. If the worry persists, that is a reason to
  refer, not to start a supplement.
- Weight loss in advanced dementia. Once the trajectory is recognised and explained, refer for a
  goals-of-care conversation instead of reaching for a tube.
- Swallowing difficulty (dysphagia). A common ward practice to watch is routinely thickening fluids
  for dysphagia. The evidence for routine thickening in dementia is weak: it can reduce aspiration
  in the moment, but its longer-term effects are uncertain [@flynn2018cochranethickening]. Recognise
  the practice and refer to a speech therapist, who sets the texture level, instead of assuming it is needed.

The recognise-and-refer approach, and the malnutrition screening behind it, are set out in the
[*Undernutrition & malnutrition*](undernutrition-malnutrition.qmd) chapter. (The wider referral map,
who does what across the multidisciplinary team, is in the
[*Interprofessional practice, referral and looking after yourself*](interprofessional-referral.qmd) chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with advanced dementia has trouble swallowing, and the ward plans routine thickened fluids. What should the generalist do instead?
The evidence for routinely thickening fluids for dysphagia is weak. Recognise it as a common ward
practice, not an established need, and refer to speech therapy instead of assuming thickening is
required.
:::

## What should a patient worried about dementia be told? {#sec-close}

Take the fear seriously, then cover four points:

1. Lead with vascular risk, because what is good for the heart is good for the brain.
2. Offer a Mediterranean-style pattern as a sensible, low-risk choice, while being clear that it is
   not a proven cure.
3. Steer away from brain supplements, which cost money and can occasionally cause harm.
4. Add the non-dietary measures with good supporting evidence, especially activity and getting hearing and
   vision corrected.

If the same family later returns with a relative who is losing weight in advanced dementia, the kind,
evidence-based answer is careful hand feeding for comfort, not a tube, with a referral for a proper conversation about goals.

## The Singapore context {#sec-singapore}

Singapore is ageing quickly, and dementia is common: about 1 in 11 residents aged 60 and over live with
it, and about half of community dementia is still undiagnosed [@subramaniam2025wisedecade]. That
undiagnosed half is the argument for the generalist's recognise-and-refer role. Locally,
dementia is commoner in Indian than Chinese residents. Indian residents in the survey also reported
more stroke, and the authors suggest the heavier cardiovascular risk seen in South Asian populations as
one explanation, although diagnosed diabetes and hypertension were not themselves linked to dementia
in that survey [@subramaniam2025wisedecade]. "Brain health is vascular health", which rests on the
wider evidence, is a message that fits national diabetes and hypertension efforts.

Two local realities shape counselling. The first is a large local market in over-the-counter "brain
tonics" (ginkgo, fish oil and traditional tonics). Being sold in a pharmacy does not make a product
proven or approved for dementia.

The second is a set of local socio-cultural findings. In a multi-ethnic Singapore cohort, overall diet
quality is associated with better cognition [@huangx2023singaporemec], and regular curry (curcumin) intake has
been associated with lower rates of new cognitive impairment in older Singaporeans [@lu2025curry]. The
curry finding generates a hypothesis; it is not a prescription. Local programmes such as the
SINGER study are adapting the multidomain approach to Singaporean food and life [@chew2021singerpilot].

## Practise: "what should I eat so I don't get dementia?" {#sec-case}

A 52-year-old whose mother has dementia asks you what diet will prevent it. Her blood pressure is
raised and her fasting glucose is in the prediabetes range. She has read that the MIND diet halves
Alzheimer's risk, and she wants a supplement recommendation. Counsel her truthfully, without offering
false hope. The case branches according to your choices.
